## Proof

**Claim.** Yes. Strong convergence implies weak convergence in any Banach space (in fact in any normed space). The weak compactness of $K$ is not needed for the conclusion.

**Setup.** Let $E$ be a Banach space and let $(x_n)_{n\ge 1}$ be a sequence in $E$ with $\|x_n - x\| \to 0$ for some $x \in E$. We must show $x_n \rightharpoonup x$, i.e. for every continuous linear functional $f \in E^*$,
$$f(x_n) \to f(x).$$

**Argument.** Fix an arbitrary $f \in E^*$. By definition of the dual norm, $|f(y)| \le \|f\|_{E^*}\,\|y\|$ for every $y \in E$. Applying this to $y = x_n - x$,
$$\bigl|f(x_n) - f(x)\bigr| = \bigl|f(x_n - x)\bigr| \le \|f\|_{E^*}\,\|x_n - x\|.$$

Since $f$ is continuous, $\|f\|_{E^*} < \infty$ is a fixed finite constant. Since $x_n \to x$ strongly, $\|x_n - x\| \to 0$. Therefore the right-hand side tends to $0$, and so
$$\bigl|f(x_n) - f(x)\bigr| \to 0, \qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad f(x_n) \to f(x).$$

Because $f \in E^*$ was arbitrary, this is exactly the definition of $x_n \rightharpoonup x$.

**Remark on the hypotheses.** The assumption $K$ weakly compact and $(x_n) \subset K$ guarantees that the strong limit $x$ also lies in $K$ (weakly compact sets are weakly closed by weak compactness implying weak sequential compactness plus the Eberlein–Šmulian theorem, and weakly closed sets are norm-closed; equivalently, weakly compact sets are norm-closed, so the norm-limit $x$ of points in $K$ stays in $K$). But the implication "strong $\Rightarrow$ weak" itself uses only the continuity of each $f \in E^*$ and holds for **every** strongly convergent sequence in **every** normed space, with no compactness hypothesis required.

**Conclusion.** Strong convergence always implies weak convergence: $\|x_n - x\|\to 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; x_n \rightharpoonup x$.

### PROOF COMPLETE
